lead: An LED is a forward-biased p-n junction that turns injected electrons into spontaneous photons. Its chip structure decides how many photons escape, and its efficiency decides how much optical power reaches a fiber. LEDs are used in short-distance links, local area networks, sensors and displays because they are cheap, reliable and need simple drive circuits. This chapter covers surface emitters (planar, dome and the high-radiance Burrus type) and edge emitters, then the efficiencies, I-P curve, spectrum, modulation bandwidth and temperature behaviour that set their use.
prereq: You need spontaneous emission and direct-bandgap recombination from 3.1; numerical aperture, from the study of light propagation in fibers, is used later in 3.6.

blocks.text: An LED is a forward-biased p-n junction. In a direct-bandgap semiconductor such as GaAs, electrons and holes recombine spontaneously and release photons. A double heterostructure places a thin active layer between wider-bandgap p and n confining layers. This traps carriers in the active layer and improves injection. The chip shape then decides how light leaves.

A planar LED is the simplest surface emitter. The active layer sits near the top surface and light exits through that surface. Total internal reflection traps much of the light because the semiconductor has a high refractive index. A dome LED shapes the chip into a hemisphere or adds a dome lens. Rays meet the surface more nearly at right angles, so more light escapes.

A higher-radiance surface emitter, called a Burrus LED in some syllabi, uses a small active area and a substrate window or well so light leaves from one face. It gives a small, bright emitting spot and couples well to a fiber. An edge emitter LED guides light along a stripe to a cleaved edge. Its emitting area is narrow and directional, so coupling is better than a simple planar LED. It still emits spontaneous light, not laser light.

Four efficiencies are easy to mix. Internal quantum efficiency η<sub>int</sub> is the number of photons generated in the active region per electron injected. Extraction efficiency η<sub>extraction</sub> is the number of photons escaping the chip per photon generated inside. External quantum efficiency η<sub>ext</sub> is the number of photons escaping per electron injected:
ηint = Nph(int)/Ne, ηext = ηint × ηextraction, ηpower = Pout/(I V)

N<sub>ph</sub>(int) is photons generated per second; N<sub>e</sub> is electrons injected per second; P<sub>out</sub> is escaping optical power in W; I is forward current in A; V is forward voltage in V. η<sub>power</sub> is wall-plug power efficiency.

Power efficiency includes electrical losses, so it is lower than η<sub>ext</sub>. The I-P curve plots P<sub>out</sub> against I. Once the diode conducts, the curve is close to a straight line through the origin, because every injected electron has the same chance of giving an escaping photon. The slope is:
E is photon energy in J; e = 1.60×10⁻¹⁹ C is the electron charge.

Linear power against current lets you modulate an LED by changing its drive current. A dome LED with η<sub>int</sub> = 0.70 and η<sub>extraction</sub> = 0.20 has η<sub>ext</sub> = 0.14; 14% of injected electrons give escaping photons. The rest become heat or trapped light.

Both factors can be found from device data. With radiative lifetime τ<sub>r</sub> and non-radiative lifetime τ<sub>nr</sub>, the total carrier lifetime τ obeys 1/τ = 1/τ<sub>r</sub> + 1/τ<sub>nr</sub>, and η<sub>int</sub> = τ/τ<sub>r</sub>. The optical power made inside the chip is then:

blocks.where: P<sub>int</sub> is internal optical power in W; hc/qλ is the photon energy in eV written as volts; I is drive current in A.

blocks.text: A flat chip loses most of this. Only rays inside the critical-angle cone reach air, and Fresnel reflection takes part of those, so the extraction efficiency of a flat surface emitting into air is about η<sub>extraction</sub> ≈ 1/[n(n + 1)²], where n is the semiconductor index. For n = 3.6 that is only 1.3%, which is why domes, textured surfaces and index-matched epoxy exist.

An LED emits over a band of wavelengths, not one line. Recombination involves a spread of carrier energies and a thermal distribution, so the spectrum has a full width at half maximum of tens of nanometres. This width causes chromatic dispersion in a fiber (treated with fiber signal degradation), so LEDs suit short links.

Speed is limited by the carrier lifetime τ. Driven at frequency f, the optical output falls as P(f)/P(0) = 1/√(1 + (2πfτ)²). The electrical 3 dB bandwidth, where the detected electrical power halves, is f<sub>3dB</sub> = 1/(2πτ); the optical 3 dB bandwidth, where the optical power halves, is √3 times larger. A shorter lifetime means faster modulation. LEDs reach tens to a few hundred MHz, well below a laser diode.

Temperature changes both power and wavelength. As temperature rises, non-radiative recombination increases, so output power falls. The bandgap shrinks, so the peak wavelength shifts to longer wavelengths. Drive circuits use temperature compensation or a monitor photodiode when output must stay steady.

examples.question: A dome LED has internal quantum efficiency 0.70 and extraction efficiency 0.20. It is driven by a forward current of 50 mA. Each emitted photon has energy 1.4 eV. Take e = 1.60×10⁻¹⁹ C and 1 eV = 1.60×10⁻¹⁹ J. Find (a) the number of photons generated per second inside the chip, (b) the number leaving the chip per second, and (c) the external optical power in mW.
steps: Convert current: I = 50 mA = 50×10⁻³ A = 0.050 A.
Electrons injected per second = I/e = 0.050/(1.60×10⁻¹⁹) = 3.125×10¹⁷ s⁻¹.
Photons generated inside = η<sub>int</sub> × electrons/s = 0.70 × 3.125×10¹⁷ = 2.1875×10¹⁷ s⁻¹.
Photons escaping = η<sub>extraction</sub> × photons inside = 0.20 × 2.1875×10¹⁷ = 4.375×10¹⁶ s⁻¹. External quantum efficiency = 0.70 × 0.20 = 0.14.
P<sub>out</sub> = escaping photons/s × photon energy = 4.375×10¹⁶ × 2.24×10⁻¹⁹ = 9.80×10⁻³ W = 9.80 mW.
examples.answer: The external optical power is about 9.8 mW.

examples.question: A double-heterostructure LED emits at 0.85 µm. Its radiative lifetime is 50 ns and its non-radiative lifetime is 80 ns, and it is driven at 30 mA. The chip surface is flat, with refractive index 3.6, and emits into air. Find (a) the internal quantum efficiency, (b) the internal optical power, (c) the power that leaves the chip, and (d) the electrical 3 dB modulation bandwidth. Use h = 6.63×10⁻³⁴ J s, c = 3.00×10⁸ m/s, q = 1.60×10⁻¹⁹ C.
steps: Photon energy: hc/(qλ) = (6.63×10⁻³⁴ × 3.00×10⁸)/(1.60×10⁻¹⁹ × 0.85×10⁻⁶) = 1.4625 eV, so each electron that recombines radiatively gives 1.4625 V × q of light.
Bandwidth: f<sub>3dB</sub> = 1/(2π × 30.8×10⁻⁹ s) = 5.17×10⁶ Hz = 5.17 MHz (electrical); the optical 3 dB bandwidth is √3 × 5.17 = 8.96 MHz.
examples.answer: η<sub>int</sub> = 0.615, P<sub>int</sub> = 27.0 mW, only 0.354 mW (1.3%) leaves the flat chip, and the electrical 3 dB bandwidth is 5.17 MHz.

traps: Do not multiply by extraction efficiency twice. External efficiency already contains η<sub>int</sub> and η<sub>extraction</sub>; use P<sub>out</sub> = η<sub>ext</sub> (I/e) E once.
Keep current in amperes and photon energy in joules: 50 mA is 0.050 A, and 1 eV = 1.60×10⁻¹⁹ J.
External quantum efficiency and power efficiency are different. η<sub>ext</sub> counts photons per electron; η<sub>power</sub> divides optical watts by electrical watts.
f<sub>3dB</sub> = 1/(2πτ) is the electrical 3 dB bandwidth. The optical 3 dB bandwidth is √3 times larger; say which one you give.
An edge emitter LED is not a laser. It is still spontaneous emission; laser action needs feedback and threshold, covered in laser action.

quiz.q: Define internal quantum efficiency of an LED.
quiz.a: It is the number of photons generated in the active region per electron injected into the diode.

quiz.q: Why does a planar LED have lower extraction efficiency than a dome LED?
quiz.a: In a planar LED many rays hit the top surface beyond the critical angle and suffer total internal reflection. The dome shape makes rays meet the surface more nearly normally, so fewer are trapped.

quiz.q: An LED has η<sub>int</sub> = 0.80, η<sub>extraction</sub> = 0.25, forward current 40 mA and photon energy 2.0 eV. Find the external optical power in mW. Take e = 1.60×10⁻¹⁹ C and 1 eV = 1.60×10⁻¹⁹ J.
quiz.a: η<sub>ext</sub> = 0.80×0.25 = 0.20. Electrons/s = 0.040/(1.60×10⁻¹⁹) = 2.5×10¹⁷ s⁻¹. Escaping photons/s = 0.20×2.5×10¹⁷ = 5.0×10¹⁶ s⁻¹. Photon energy = 2.0×1.60×10⁻¹⁹ = 3.2×10⁻¹⁹ J. P<sub>out</sub> = 5.0×10¹⁶×3.2×10⁻¹⁹ = 1.6×10⁻² W = 16 mW.

quiz.q: Give two reasons why an LED's output power falls as temperature rises.
quiz.a: First, non-radiative recombination and carrier leakage over the heterobarriers rise with temperature, so η<sub>int</sub> falls and fewer photons are made per electron; this is the main effect. Second, the bandgap shrinks, so each photon carries less energy (and the peak moves to a longer wavelength); the same photon rate then carries slightly less power.

quiz.q: State the difference between external quantum efficiency and power efficiency.
quiz.a: External quantum efficiency is escaping photons per injected electron. Power efficiency is emitted optical power divided by electrical input power (I V).

quiz.q: An LED has a straight I-P line through the origin with slope 0.20 W/A. Find the optical power at a drive current of 30 mA.
Why does an edge emitter LED couple better to a fiber than a planar LED?
quiz.a: Its emitting area is narrow and its light is guided along a stripe, so the output has a smaller area and a narrower angular spread. This raises radiance and matches the fiber core and numerical aperture better.

beyond: Not for the exam. LEDs now appear in visible-light communication, where room lights carry data, and in plastic-optical-fiber links inside cars and homes. Blue and white GaN LEDs changed lighting, and micro-LEDs are being developed for displays. Researchers work on improving extraction with photonic crystals and surface textures, and on faster LEDs by shortening carrier lifetime. Search terms: Burrus LED, resonant-cavity LED, micro-LED, visible light communication.
